title: Chapter 11.  Current Developments — The Situation Since May 2023

blocks.content: This chapter addresses recent and highly significant events in Manipur factually and with appropriate care, given the sensitivity and continuing human impact of the situation described. Candidates should understand this as an evolving, complex situation involving multiple communities and perspectives, not a simple narrative with a single cause or resolution.

Ethnic violence broke out in Manipur in early May 2023, primarily between sections of the Meitei community (concentrated in the Imphal Valley) and sections of the Kuki-Zo community (concentrated in the hill districts, particularly Churachandpur), following tensions that had been building around several contested issues, including a Manipur High Court order in March 2023 directing the state government to consider recommending Scheduled Tribe status for the Meitei community, opposition to which had already prompted a 'Tribal Solidarity March' organised by hill-tribal groups on 3 May 2023, during which clashes broke out and rapidly escalated.

Underlying and contributing tensions cited by various analysts and community representatives include long-standing disputes over land rights and forest-reserve boundaries, differing community perspectives on immigration and demographic change (particularly concerning migration from Myanmar following that country's own internal conflict), and pre-existing political and economic grievances between hill and valley communities — candidates should note that different communities and observers offer differing emphases on these underlying causes, and this remains a matter of ongoing discussion rather than a single agreed narrative.

The violence that followed resulted in a substantial number of deaths (widely reported figures cite over 250 people killed across the conflict's duration) and large-scale displacement (tens of thousands of people, from both communities, displaced from their homes into relief camps), along with significant destruction of property, places of worship, and infrastructure in various parts of the state — among the most serious instances of sustained inter-community conflict in India in recent years.

★ EXAM POINT: This topic requires care in exam answers: state the KEY FACTS (the March 2023 High Court order, the 3 May 2023 Tribal Solidarity March, the scale of displacement/casualties) without asserting a single, one-sided account of blame, since this remains a genuinely contested and evolving situation with multiple community perspectives.

items: The Government of India deployed substantial additional central security forces to the state and, at various points, imposed internet suspensions and movement restrictions in affected areas aimed at curbing further violence and the spread of misinformation.

A broad, informal territorial and administrative separation emerged over this period between valley (Meitei-majority) and hill (largely Kuki-Zo-inhabited) areas, with significant restrictions on movement between the two zones reported by various sources — a de facto segregation that became one of the most widely reported and concerning features of the conflict's persistence.

Various rounds of peace talks, community dialogue initiatives, and government outreach efforts were attempted through this period, including engagement facilitated by central government representatives, though a comprehensive, lasting political resolution had not been achieved as of the most recent developments.

As detailed in Chapter 5, Chief Minister N. Biren Singh resigned in February 2025 amid sustained criticism of his government's handling of the crisis, leading to President's Rule (13 February 2025 - 4 February 2026).

blocks.content: The Situation Since the Return of Elected Government (February 2026)

Following the revocation of President's Rule and the swearing-in of Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh's cross-community cabinet (Chapter 5) on 4 February 2026, the new government undertook early confidence-building measures, including a formal engagement meeting with the Kuki-Zo Council held in Guwahati on 21 March 2026 — reported as the first such formal engagement between state government leaders and Kuki-Zo representatives in nearly three years.

Despite these initial steps, various subsequent reports through mid-2026 indicated that durable peace, economic normalisation, and full restoration of public confidence across communities remained incomplete challenges facing the new government, with continuing concern among observers about the risk of renewed instability if reconciliation efforts did not produce sustained, visible progress.

Given the genuinely live and evolving nature of this situation, candidates preparing for current-affairs-linked exams should treat any specific details beyond the core established facts and dates presented here as subject to change, and should consult the latest available news sources closer to their exam date for the most up-to-date picture.

items: Ethnic violence began early May 2023, following a March 2023 Manipur High Court order on Meitei ST-status consideration and the 3 May 2023 'Tribal Solidarity March'.
Widely reported figures: over 250 deaths and tens of thousands displaced across the conflict's duration; significant property/infrastructure destruction.
A broad, informal valley-hills territorial separation, with movement restrictions between zones, became a persistent and widely reported feature of the conflict.
N. Biren Singh resigned 9 Feb 2025; President's Rule 13 Feb 2025 - 4 Feb 2026; new cross-community government under Yumnam Khemchand Singh from 4 Feb 2026 (Chapter 5).
A first formal government-Kuki-Zo Council engagement meeting was held in Guwahati on 21 March 2026; durable, comprehensive resolution remained an ongoing challenge as of mid-2026.
